## 2. Symbol Analysis

**1. The Numerology of 15:**

#### 1 + 5 = 6

5 represents freedom, change, and sensory impulses.

Originally, it is the energy that breaks rules and pursues experiences, but in the Devil card, this freedom has gone astray and turned into indulgence. It is the unrestrained pursuit of money, power, and pleasure—a state where desire is out of control.

1 symbolizes the self, willpower, and creativity.

Here, this "I" becomes narrow and selfish—not to create, but to possess; not to connect, but to control. It only cares about what I want, without considering "we" or "everyone."

1 + 5 = 6, and 6 is the Lovers card—a card about love, choice, and harmonious union. The Devil card is like a fallen version of the Lovers card. What could have been a sincere, equal relationship instead chooses desire over love, possession over connection. Despite having the ability to move toward a beautiful union, it becomes trapped in a seemingly free but actually binding cage due to indulgence in senses and selfish desires. This is not true intimacy but a mistaken union.

![Tarot illustration](https://internal-api-drive-stream.feishu.cn/space/api/box/stream/download/authcode/?code=NjdhYWYyMTNiNTNiOGY5ZjBkZmMxOTU4MzE5MjY4ZDdfYTEzNmRiMWUxYzQ2MmNmMzk1MDQ3NmY3YTJiNzQ3YWVfSUQ6NzYxOTIzNDQ1OTY5MjE5MDkzOF8xNzgyMTgxNDQ5OjE3ODIyNjc4NDlfVjM)

#### 3 x 5 = 15

3 represents intellect, creativity, and thought; 5 represents the five senses and the material world. Normally, the intellect should guide the senses, helping us discern what is worth pursuing and what is just fleeting stimulation. But in the Devil card, this relationship is reversed—the senses become the master, and the intellect becomes its servant. You start using your cleverness to make excuses: "I'll just buy it one more time," "It's no big deal," "Everyone else does it"... In reality, your heart is led by desire, yet you think you are clear-headed.

Ultimately, the Devil card is not trying to scare you but to remind you: true freedom is never indulgence, but the ability to make conscious choices even after seeing desire clearly.

**2. Belongs to the Earth Element**

The Earth element originally symbolizes wealth, body, and security—tangible things. But in the Devil card, it represents that once you treat possession as your sole life goal, you become controlled by these things. Like the chains around the necks of the figures in the card, which look like they are guarding their property or status but have actually become shackles imprisoning themselves.

Desire under the influence of the Earth element becomes especially concrete, slowly turning from a thought into a deeply rooted habit, such as addiction, overworking, or compulsive shopping. At this point, people tend to focus only on immediate benefits and pleasures, forgetting what their inner self truly needs and unable to see broader possibilities.

**3. Astrological Correspondence: Capricorn**

Astrologically, the Devil card corresponds to Capricorn, whose ruling planet is Saturn—a planet representing limitation, responsibility, and reality.

Capricorn itself pursues achievement, status, and control, which is not wrong in itself. But the Devil card shows its shadow side: ruthless pursuit of success at any cost, sacrificing feelings, conscience, even turning oneself into a cold machine.

The half-human, half-goat figure in the card is like a goat climbing recklessly upward, eyes fixed only on the summit, indifferent to what it tramples or sacrifices.

Behind this obsession lies deep fear—fear of failure, loss of control, and loss itself. So many would rather stay in bad relationships or jobs than risk change, because familiar pain seems safer than unknown freedom. But this sense of security is an illusion, precisely the bait the Devil is best at.

**4. Hebrew Letter: Ayin (Eye)**

This card corresponds to the Hebrew letter Ayin, meaning "eye."

This is interesting—it doesn’t mean you cannot see, but that you "see wrongly." Your eyes are blinded by materialism, only able to see money, desire, and short-term gain, but unable to see spiritual freedom and inner light. More deeply, the "devil" you see is often a projection of your own fears or desires. You think the outside world is binding you, but the shackles are ones you put on yourself. True liberation may begin by changing your perspective on the world.

## 3. Case Studies

## 1. Qi Tongwei in "In the Name of the People" — The Deadliest is Falling While Awake

Is Qi Tongwei miserable? Yes.

Born into a poor family, a drug enforcement hero, shot three times, and what happened? Because he refused to bow to the powerful, he was directly sent to a remote township as the director of the judicial office.

At that moment, he saw through it all: "A hero is nothing before absolute power!"

So, he made a decision: **to kneel.**

He knelt before the old party secretary’s funeral altar, proposing to Liang Lu, whom he did not love.

With that kneel, he sold his dignity, tore up his ideals, and exchanged it for a ticket to cling to the Zhao family’s power.

**The Devil card:** The chains are not forcibly put on you by others; you voluntarily put your hands into the lock for that little "future." He was not blinded; he sold himself to the devil with his own hands.

Later, he became the public security director, lived in a mountain villa, raised police dogs, played golf, and looked very prosperous.

But was he happy? No, he lived in fear—fear of being reported, fear of losing his position, fear of returning to being a poor boy.

Did he turn back? No.

He sank deeper: killing to silence, corruption, manipulating the political-legal system.

This is like the man and woman in the Devil card—the chains are loose and could be removed anytime, but they **do not want to leave.** Because they have grown accustomed to this "life nurtured by power," thinking this is what life is.

He loved to say: "I want to be the master of heaven and earth!"

It sounds tragic and inspiring, right?

But this is actually the most dangerous illusion of the Devil card: **using a tragic narrative of "fighting fate" to package selfish desires; using the slogan of "grassroots uprising" to cover up plundering others.**

He treats corruption as compensation owed by fate, harming others as a necessary means to climb up.

This is not struggle; it is self-justification after selling the soul to desire.

In the end, he was besieged at Lone Eagle Ridge—the place where he was once wounded and honored.

He shot himself, shouting before death: "To hell with the heavens!"

Note, he never repented. He did not see himself as a great sinner; he only hated that he lost to fate.

**The Devil card never promises redemption; it only shows one truth:** When you sell your soul to desire, the end is inevitably self-destruction.

**Let’s compare with the card imagery, perfectly fitting:**

- **Goat-headed Devil (the tempter):** Represents the powerful system embodied by Zhao Lichun and Liang Lu, using "future prospects" as bait to lure him in.

- **Chained man and woman (voluntary slavery):** Qi Tongwei and Gao Xiaoqin. The two collude, indulging in the prison of power and lust, neither willing to escape.

- **Downward burning torch:** His ambition is like that inverted torch, illuminating no one but burning himself to ashes.

- **Horns and tail (beastification):** From a passionate hero to the "political traitor" in Sha Ruijin’s words, his humanity has long been distorted.

- **Dark background (no way out):** He wanted to redeem himself (e.g., investing in Dafeng Factory), but his sins were too deep, and there was no turning back.

Qi Tongwei’s tragedy is not that fate was unfair, but that he **voluntarily put on those shackles.**

He clearly had hands, feet, and talent but chose to believe "only by colluding can one succeed."

**The scariest prison is not a door locked by others, but that you hold the key yet choose never to open the door because you are addicted to the "comfort" inside.**

Qi Tongwei won half the game but lost his whole life. This is the price of "falling while awake."

## 2. Qu Wanting — Slave to Desire

The two people on the Devil card are chained, seemingly unable to move, but the chains are loose—they **do not want to break free.**

Qu Wanting lives in a mansion in Canada, drives a Maserati, and pursues a music career. Where does all this confidence come from? It all comes from her mother Zhang Mingjie’s embezzlement of over 98 million yuan!

This money was the resettlement fund for 566 laid-off workers! It was their lifeline, their heating fee in the cold winter. Some committed suicide out of despair from heating cuts; some froze to death in Harbin’s winter.

Qu Wanting’s infamous quote is harsh: "My mother gave me the best life, no matter how she got it."

This is the core metaphor of the Devil card: **She enjoys freedom built on the blood and tears of countless people.** She clearly knows the chain is tied to others’ lives but chooses to look away.

She packages herself overseas as a "Chinese-Canadian independent musician" and even served as a Vancouver tourism ambassador.

She is very much like the man and woman in the Devil card—dressed decently, even with a bit of bourgeois flair, but **her soul has long been tightly chained by desire.**

She is not a self-made independent woman; she stands on the ruins of 566 broken families singing. Her "independence" is entirely maintained by stolen money. This is like the offerings on the Devil’s altar—seemingly lofty but actually slaves to desire.

The scariest thing is not ignorance but **knowing and still doing wrong.**

After her mother’s scandal, she hid abroad, refused to return or cooperate with investigations, and instead cried injustice on social media, calling the corrupt mother a "hero."

Facing the victims’ families’ pleas, she never apologized or returned a penny of the stolen money.

Even in 2026, she tried to wear a red outfit printed with "China" to celebrate the New Year and attempt a comeback, but was widely condemned and her account was immediately banned.

This is like the people in the Devil card growing horns on their heads but thinking they look good. She has internalized this exploitative logic, treating evil as normal and silence as innocence. **She is not forced into silence; she actively chooses to stay in darkness** because admitting the truth would collapse the life built on lies.

Even now, with overseas assets frozen and life difficult, she still refuses to cut ties.

Why not return the stolen money and repent? Why not confess?

Because that is her "comfort zone." The most painful part of the Devil card is here: **The door is actually open, the key is in hand, but the locked person refuses to leave.**

Qu Wanting has the chance to repent and the ability to speak out against corruption but chooses to protect vested interests and beautify the source of evil.

The Central Commission for Discipline Inspection has long pointed out: "The children of corrupt officials enjoying overseas luxury will eventually be judged by history and the people."

Qu Wanting’s story tells us:

**True slavery is never forced but when you know the truth yet choose to close your eyes and keep singing for a little comfort and vanity.**
